ch. 05 · I'm the one holding the pen

a little about me

that's me!

I started in visual communication, learning how things look. Now I study why people do what they do, and design for that.

My interest in UX began far from a screen. In the third year of my bachelor's I documented Kutchi Bharat, the hand embroidery of Kutch, and spent days in the villages where it is made. I sat with craftswomen who sell their own work, some who stitch for NGOs and some whose pieces go to museums, and listened to how each of them works, what they are paid for and what gets in their way.

That research changed how I see design. The same craft meant something different to every woman, and the systems around them, from the NGO's order sheet to the museum's brief, shaped their days as much as the thread did. I came home wanting to design those systems with the same care they give to a single stitch. The documentation and the documentary are on Behance.

I still start every project the same way: with people, before pixels. When someone knows what's fresh, what's next or who they're talking to, they relax, and the product gets easier to use.

Off screen you'll find me painting, running, doing yoga, hunting for good coffee and croissants, or saying hello to every dog I pass.

Redesigning the JioCare chatbot ∙ MyJio

Making SIM porting conversations clear enough to finish.

A Double Diamond approach to SIM port retention: turning a text-only, rule-based bot into a structured, reason-aware support experience.

Role
UX research, conversation design, prototyping
Timeline
Jan 2026
Guide
Dhaval Joshi, Dhirubhai Ambani University
Method
Double Diamond
Platform
MyJio app, JioCare chatbot
Status
Academic project

overview

JioCare is the in-app support chatbot inside MyJio. It helps users with telecom-related tasks: recharges, network issues, SIM management and account queries.

The redesign focused on one central scenario: a user who opens the chatbot and says, “I want to port my SIM.” It is a retention-critical moment, emotionally loaded for the user and commercially significant for the business, which made it the sharpest lens for testing whether a redesigned conversation could balance user trust with business goals.

Objective: redesign the JioCare chatbot experience to deliver structured, trust-building conversations, with a focus on SIM port scenarios where emotional stakes and business outcomes are highest.

01 – the gap

Five recurring breakdowns in the current chatbot.

  1. No functional user guideUsers are dropped into a chat with no clear sense of what the bot can and cannot do.
  2. Conversations lack logical structureReplies follow keywords rather than a guided path, so users rarely know where they stand.
  3. Repetitive responsesIdentical generic answers appear regardless of what the user actually asked.
  4. No visible task progressMulti-step requests give no signal of what has been done or what comes next.
  5. SIM port queries are confusingThe most consequential request in the bot receives the weakest and most confusing guidance.

02 – approach

A four-phase Double Diamond: diverging and converging twice, to find the right problem before building the right solution.

Discover · Empathise

Observed real chatbot behaviour and recorded user pain points first-hand.

Define · Reframe

Reframed the problem from a service-leadership lens, not just a UX lens.

Develop · Ideate

Generated solutions through structured methods: reverse ideation, brand swap, form swap and AI-assisted ideation.

Deliver · Prototype

Built a working hybrid voice + text chatbot prototype.

03 – why SIM porting

SIM porting became the sharpest lens to test whether a redesigned system could balance user trust with business goals.

Retention-critical

The highest churn-risk moment in the user journey.

Poor structure

The current flow offers no guided path or clarity.

Measurable outcome

Success can be tracked through churn-reduction metrics.

Emotionally loaded

The decision involves frustration and distrust, not just a task.

04 – what the evidence showed

The problem isn’t simply that the bot gives wrong answers. The conversation itself lacks structure and continuity.

01 · Missing guide

The user guide is unreachable or non-existent within the chatbot.

02 · Unstructured flow

Conversations meander, with no clear steps or resolution path.

03 · Repetition

Identical generic responses regardless of the user’s query.

04 · SIM port gap

Porting queries receive the weakest and most confusing guidance.

05 – problem to direction

Defining the problem, the reasons behind it and the direction the solution should take.

Problem

Users interacting with JioCare, especially around SIM porting, encounter a bot that repeats itself, loses conversational context and offers no clarity on where they stand in the process.

Why it happens

The bot is optimised for deflection and containment, not resolution. There is no reasoning layer, so it cannot adapt when a user wants to port. And the text-only, single-turn design loses context between messages.

Solution direction

A support experience that maintains conversational continuity, avoids repetition and enables meaningful resolution, while still respecting business constraints such as automation-first support and retention incentives.

06 – stakeholder perspectives

Three voices with different, and sometimes competing, definitions of success.

Fast, clear answer without repetition. I’m frustrated by dead ends, generic responses and having to restart the conversation.

End user

Reduce operational load without silently increasing churn. The bot needs to handle retention intelligently, not just deflect queries.

Head of Customer Relations

Keep the redesign feasible within existing constraints. Any solution must work within the current rule-based architecture without a full platform rebuild.

Developer

07 – how might we

How might we create a structured support experience that maintains continuity, avoids repetition and enables meaningful resolution, while balancing automation with business constraints?

This single statement held the three stakeholder needs in tension and became the brief for ideation.

08 – ideation

Multiple ideation techniques were used to move from “what’s broken” to “what could work”.

  1. Reverse ideationListed what not to do: repetitive loops, generic replies, no memory. Then used that list as a checklist against every new idea.
  2. Brand swap · AdobeIf Adobe’s cancellation flow had to handle a Jio SIM port request, what would it do differently?
  3. Form swapConverted the chatbot from text-only into a hybrid voice + text virtual assistant.
  4. AI assistanceUsed AI tooling to assist with conversational flow testing and prototype logic.

09 – brand swap deep-dive

A telecom port-out and a subscription cancellation are the same moment: a user has decided to leave a paid service. Adobe’s retention flow became the benchmark.

Borrowed · Offer before exit

The user sees real-value alternatives before the cancellation completes, not a flat “are you sure?”

Borrowed · Reason-aware framing

Retention works best when the alternative answers the user’s actual reason for leaving.

Borrowed · A pause, not a wall

The offer creates a moment to reconsider without removing the user’s ability to proceed.

Deliberately not borrowed · Friction

Cancellation flows are often criticised for adding friction. The JioCare redesign keeps the offer and removes the friction: porting steps are always one clear tap away.

10 – how it translates to JioCare

Each Adobe-style idea, mapped to its JioCare adaptation.

  1. Retention offer before cancelling25% off next 2 recharges when the user says “I want to port my SIM”
  2. Offer matched to the user’s reasonOffers and actions depend on the reason selected (reason-based intelligence)
  3. Easy, honest exitClear porting steps: SMS PORT to 1900, receive UPC, visit the new operator
  4. Bring users back laterWelcome-back offer: cashback on first recharge plus free SIM activation

11 – the shift

Before: a text-only chatbot. After: a hybrid voice + text assistant. The resulting prototype features:

Hybrid voice and text interactionContinuous chat history, no lost contextReason-based retention logicResponsive buttons for lower-friction decisions

12 – user flow

The redesigned conversation, from the first message to a graceful exit.

  1. Open MyJio → JioCareThe user navigates to the chatbot and says “I want to port my SIM”.
  2. Limited-time offerThe bot shows a discount offer: 25% off the next 2 recharges. The user chooses.
  3. Accepts the offerThe system applies the 25% discount, shows a confirmation message, and the user is retained.
  4. Continues with portThe bot displays the porting steps: send SMS PORT with the mobile number to 1900, receive the UPC code, visit the new operator with UPC and ID.
  5. Welcome-back offer20% cashback on the first recharge and free SIM activation, valid within 7 days of reactivation.
  6. Graceful exitThe flow ends without pressure and with no dark patterns.

13 – design rules behind the flow

Four rules that govern every branch of the conversation.

  1. Reason-based intelligenceOffers and actions depend on the reason selected. Applied in retention strategy mapping.
  2. Hybrid accessibilityVoice and text are supported equally. Applied in the interface and interaction model.
  3. No repetitive loopsAvoid repeating generic responses. Applied in fallback handling and confirmations.
  4. Win-back logicEncourage return without pressure. Applied in the welcome-back offer.

14 – screen annotations

What the interface does differently.

Clean entry point

Low visual noise, with immediate access to voice or text input.

Continuous chat history

Previous context is preserved: no repetition, no restarting.

Persistent visual identity

An avatar and status give the bot a consistent, trusted presence.

15 – conclusion

From answering questions to understanding intent.

Conversation structure

A clear arc from greeting to resolution removes anxiety and repetition through persistent chat history.

User trust

Transparency about what is happening and what comes next builds confidence at every step.

Reason-based logic

Understanding why a user is leaving is the foundation of effective, non-manipulative retention.

Transparent retention

Honest offers, clearly explained, are more effective than hidden nudges or dark patterns.

16 – what I learned

The existing chatbot lacked conversational structure, repeated generic responses and failed to guide users clearly, especially in high-stakes moments like SIM porting.

The redesign shows how a rule-based support system can become a structured, user-centred conversational experience without a platform rebuild: continuity through persistent history, clarity through reason-based logic, and trust through transparent, pressure-free retention offers.

The Everyday Vegetable Market ∙ Design research · Field study · UX research

What would help customers trust what's fresh, and vendors know what will sell?

A field study of Sector 21 Vegetable Market, Gandhinagar: customer behaviour, vendor practices, freshness, pricing and time pressure, and a lightweight digital layer that supports what already works.

at a glance

3gates connecting customers to the market
3study sessions across the day
4questions I went in with
6insights the market taught me

01 – prologueA vegetable market looks simple from the outside.

Choose, weigh, pay, leave. But spending time inside it revealed a more complicated experience.

Freshness, price, negotiation, browsing and time pressure all shape a purchase, and customers often leave still unsure. At the same time, vendors manage daily stock without always knowing exactly how much they will sell. Two sides of one market, each guessing.

“I wanted to understand what happens behind this everyday transaction.”

02 – the settingSector 21 Vegetable Market, Gandhinagar.

The market is organised around individual vendor spaces known as otala, with three gates connecting customers to the marketplace.

Three study sessions across the day covered the morning rush, the quieter midday window and the evening wave, with conversations with vendors and customers in between.

03 – two ways of shopping

Observation: the vegetable market is not simply a place to purchase vegetables. It is also a place to evaluate, compare and discover.

Type A · The Planner

“I already know what I need.” Carries a list, looks for specific vegetables, moves between vendors and wants to finish quickly.

Type B · The Explorer

“Let me see what’s fresh.” Arrives without a list, browses different vendors, inspects vegetables and makes decisions in the market.

04 – what I wanted to understandI went into the market with four questions.

Field observation across 08:00–10:00 AM, 10:00 AM–02:00 PM and 04:00–06:00 PM, plus conversations with vendors and customers.

  1. How do customers decide what vegetables to buy?
  2. How do customers judge freshness?
  3. How does bargaining influence the buying experience?
  4. How do vendors manage their daily stock?

05 – a day in the marketThe market changes throughout the day.

Relative activity, as observed on site.

08–10 AM · The Morning Rush

Highest activity. Customers arrived with shopping lists as well as without. Fresh stock was highly visible.

10 AM–2 PM · The Quieter Window

Activity reduced. Customers had more time to browse while vendors continued selling existing stock.

4–6 PM · The Evening Wave

Customer activity increased again during the evening period.

Weekends · Busier across all hours

Weekends were observed to have significantly higher activity across all hours.

06 – customer voicesSometimes, appearance isn’t enough.

Three customers, three things the market revealed.

Ye sundar dikhta hai par andar kharab hoga. Kal ka maal lagta hai. — Freshness is perceived through inspection, but confidence is not guaranteed.

Customer 01

Itna to kam kar do price bhaiya. — Price is not only a number. It is part of the trust and negotiation experience.

Customer 02

A regular morning shopper sometimes still finds vegetables that do not meet expectations. — Visiting during a preferred time does not always guarantee perceived freshness.

Customer 03

07 – looking at the vendorThe customer’s uncertainty is only one side of the story.

Nikulbhai, Otala #54, Madadev Vegetable Otala, with 25–30 years of experience in the market.

A day, as he lives it: bring stock → display → sell → sort remaining → continue selling → discard remaining. What happens when demand is difficult to predict?

A second vendor with a long family association with the market sells core stock, potato, onion and garlic, where customers may purchase 2–3 kg or more in a single visit. A third sells green vegetables. A digital solution cannot assume every vendor operates the same way.

08 – an unexpected research questionWinter vegetables, sold all year.

Some vegetables associated with winter were being sold throughout the year. Instead of immediately treating this as a problem, I treated it as a research question.

How do customers understand seasonal availability when vegetables appear throughout the year?

Field research is not only about finding answers. Sometimes, it is about finding better questions.

09 – what kept repeatingAfter organising observations, four themes repeatedly appeared.

The bigger pattern: customers and vendors, connected by freshness, price, time, demand, remaining stock, and uncertainty in the middle.

01 · Time

Customers experience greater activity and congestion during peak periods.

02 · Price

Bargaining is a recurring part of the customer–vendor interaction.

03 · Freshness

Customers cannot always confidently determine internal quality from appearance.

04 · Stock

Vendors have to manage vegetables that may remain unsold.

10 – key insightsSix things the market taught me.

What the observations added up to.

Freshness is perceived, not guaranteed

Customers inspect vegetables physically, but visual appearance does not always create confidence.

Bargaining is partly an information problem

When the basis for a price is not visible, negotiation becomes part of the purchase.

Time pressure is concentrated

The market becomes significantly more active during particular periods.

Customers have different shopping intentions

Some arrive with a list while others use the market to explore.

Stock uncertainty affects vendors

Unsold vegetables create a challenge for daily stock management.

Digital payment is already familiar

Frequent UPI use suggests a lightweight digital layer could fit into existing behaviour.

11 – the design questionHow might we make the vegetable-buying experience at Sector 21 Market more transparent and time-efficient, while helping vendors better understand expected demand and manage daily stock?

The goal was not to replace the physical market. The goal was to add a simple digital layer to an existing behaviour.

12 – the conceptA simple digital layer for the place Gandhinagar already trusts.

Customer journey, in seven steps.

  1. BrowseExplore today’s vegetables.
  2. CheckView price and freshness information.
  3. SelectChoose vegetables and quantities.
  4. ReserveSelect a pickup slot: 7–8 AM or 5–6 PM.
  5. ConfirmReceive order confirmation and a QR.
  6. VisitGo directly to the selected otala.
  7. Pick upScan → verify → collect.

13 – what the layer offers

Four features for customers; one flow for vendors: expected demand → stock planning → prepare → quick handover.

Pre-order

Reserve vegetables before reaching the market.

Time-slot pickup

Choose a preferred pickup window.

Price transparency

See a daily reference price alongside the vendor’s price.

Freshness info

“Harvested: Today” or “Stock age: 1 day”, updated by the vendor.

14 – the customer flowKnow what’s fresh. Pick up when it’s calm.

How a customer moves through the app: check freshness and price, reserve a calm pickup slot, then show a QR at the otala.

Open the app → browse today’s vegetables with freshness, price and vendor → product detail: fresh and price fair? → review the order → choose a pickup slot → order reserved with QR → track status → show the QR at the otala → collect and pay the vendor.

15 – the customer appFrom a vegetable you can trust to a QR you can show.

Taaza Otala, the Sector 21 digital market prototype. Freshness you can read, prices you can compare, and a pickup that skips the rush.

01 · Home

Next pickup first. The calmest time to come is the first thing customers see.

02 · Browse

Freshness on every row. Search, filter and add without leaving the list.

03 · Product detail

The research answered in one card: harvested today, updated by the vendor, with a reference price.

04 · Your order

Pickup from one named otala. Payment stays the way vendors and customers already trade.

05 · Pickup slot

Two calm windows, away from the morning rush. “A little calmer, a lot quicker.”

06 · Order reserved

A numbered order and a QR. The ticket the vendor can scan in seconds.

07 · My order

Status from placed to picked up, with the QR one tap away.

16 – the vendor flowPlan the day. Keep the market moving.

How a vendor works through the dashboard: read demand, update stock, freshness and price, publish once, then prepare and verify each order.

Open the dashboard → overview of pre-orders, value and customers → expected demand with a 7-day trend → enough stock? update today’s stock → set freshness and today’s prices against the reference range → publish → customers reserve → prepare and mark ready → scan the customer’s QR and complete pickup → daily summary feeds tomorrow’s demand.

17 – the vendor dashboardFrom a quiet morning to a verified pickup.

The dashboard for Nikulbhai Patel, Otala #54. Demand first, then stock, freshness and price, then orders and the QR scan at the counter.

Overview

Pre-orders today, order value, customers, expected demand and next pickups in one view.

Expected demand

Confirmed pre-orders per item, with a 7-day trend to plan the harvest.

Today’s stock

Available, reserved and remaining at a glance, with low-stock flags.

Update freshness

Mark harvested today or stock age. Customers see the change instantly.

Today’s prices

Set prices beside the market reference range, then publish once.

Orders and Scan QR

Open an order, prepare it, mark it ready; scan the ticket, verify, complete pickup.

18 – two sides, one marketWhere the customer and the vendor meet.

Four handovers between the vendor dashboard and the customer app.

  1. Vendor → Customer: publishes freshness and priceCustomers see “Harvested: Today” and the reference range on Browse and Detail.
  2. Customer → Vendor: reserves a pickup slotThe order appears in Expected demand and Next pickups, before the market opens.
  3. Vendor → Customer: marks the order readyMy order moves from Preparing to Ready for pickup, and the customer is notified.
  4. Customer → Vendor: shows the QRThe vendor scans it, verifies the order and completes pickup in seconds.

19 – research to featureEvery feature came from an observation.

Each observation, and the feature it led to.

  1. “The market is busiest during specific periods.”Time-slot pickup
  2. “Customers negotiate about price.”Reference-price visibility
  3. “Customers question freshness.”Freshness and stock-age information
  4. “Vendors manage unsold vegetables.”Demand visibility
  5. “Customers already use UPI.”Digital confirmation and payment familiarity

20 – validationThe next question: will people actually use it?

Three A/B tests planned on the prototype.

A/B 01 · Freshness

Tomato at ₹40/kg vs the same with “Harvested: Today, stock age under 1 day”. Does additional freshness information increase confidence?

A/B 02 · Price

Vendor price alone vs vendor price beside a reference price of ₹38/kg. Does price context reduce the need for negotiation?

A/B 03 · Pickup

Walk-in purchase vs pre-order with time-slot pickup. Does pre-ordering feel more convenient than browsing at peak time?

21 – reflectionI entered the market looking at bargaining. I left thinking about uncertainty.

Initially, bargaining appeared to be the most obvious problem. But observing customers and vendors showed that price negotiation was connected to a larger experience involving freshness, trust, time, information and stock.

The biggest learning was that the solution did not need to replace the market. It needed to support what already works.

22 – conclusionThe market doesn’t need to become fully digital. It needs better information at the right moment.

From observation, to pattern, to insight, to opportunity, to prototype.

This research transformed an everyday vegetable market into a study of time, trust, freshness, price and stock. The resulting opportunity is a lightweight digital system that connects customers and retail vendors while keeping the physical market at the centre.

the study at a glance

42riders surveyed
3ride-along observations
1.8 saverage glance in the old layout
< 1 starget glance time

01 – overview

The TVS Ronin is a modern-retro motorcycle with a round digital cluster. Riders read it in quick glances while keeping their eyes on the road.

The existing display packs speed, gear, fuel, trip, clock and ride mode into a small round face, and the most-checked information sits off-centre and in low contrast.

I redesigned the cluster around the rider's line of sight: what you check most sits where your eyes already are, in a size and contrast you can read in under a second.

02 – goals

What the redesign had to achieve.

Shorter glances

Bring the most-checked information to the centre and make it readable in under a second.

Day and night

Contrast that holds in direct sun and at night without a mode switch.

Standards-aligned

Follow ISO guidance for in-vehicle displays and use ISO symbols riders already know.

03 – research

Survey first, then on the bike.

  1. Rider survey42 Ronin and similar-bike riders. What do you check most? When do you look down? What is hard to read?
  2. Ride-alongsThree rides as pillion with a camera on the cluster, counting glances and what each glance was for.
  3. Standards reviewRead ISO 15008 (legibility of in-vehicle displays) and ISO 2575 (symbols) and turned them into a checklist.
  4. Glance analysisTimed glances on video. Speed and gear were 70% of all glances; fuel and clock were checked at stops.

04 – key insights

Three findings drove the layout.

Two numbers matter while moving

Speed and gear are almost all of the glances on the move. Everything else can wait for a stop.

Centre is faster

Riders found information at the top-centre fastest; corners cost an extra glance.

Contrast beats colour

Riders in sun could not read the thin teal text. Thick white on black read in every condition.

05 – who I designed for

A
Arjun, 29Daily commuter, 25 km a day

Rides in city traffic, checks speed and gear constantly, fuel once a day.

Goals
Know his speed without thinking
See the gear at a glance
Pain points
Glare at noon
Small fuel bar
Cluttered face
P
Priya, 35Weekend tourer

Long rides on highways, cares about range, trip distance and the time.

Goals
Range at a glance
Trip info without menus
Pain points
Night brightness
Icons she does not recognise

06 – ideation

From glance map to layout.

  1. Glance mapPlotted where each piece of information should sit based on how often it is checked and how urgent it is.
  2. Three layoutsExplored a classic dial, a split face and a centred stack. The centred stack won the glance test.
  3. Type and contrastChose a tall numeral with a thick stroke; tested white-on-black and black-on-white in sun and at night.

07 – the solution

A centred, high-contrast cluster with one job while moving and more at a stop.

Speed sits dead centre in a large numeral; gear sits just below it. Both are readable in under a second.

Fuel, range and ride mode live in a quieter ring around the edge, with ISO symbols so nothing needs reading.

At a stop, the cluster expands to show trip, clock and warnings; on the move it simplifies again.

08 – testing

Glance tests with a printed cluster on the bike.

  1. MethodMounted printouts of old and new layouts on a parked Ronin; eight riders read speed and gear from a quick glance while a stopwatch ran.
  2. ResultAverage glance to read speed fell from 1.8 s to 0.7 s. Gear was read correctly 100% of the time, up from 75%.

09 – results

Old layout versus new, in the glance test.

beforeafter
Glance to read speed1.8 s→0.7 s
Gear read correctly75%→100%
Readable in sunNo→Yes
ISO symbols usedSome→All

10 – what I learned

On a motorcycle, every extra glance is a risk, so hierarchy is a safety feature.

Designing for a glance is a different discipline from designing for a screen you hold. The whole layout came from one question: what do you need while moving?

Next I would prototype on the actual cluster hardware and test with riders at speed on a closed course.

FromIndia ∙ Mobile app · UX case study

Who do you ask when everything is new?

FromIndia is a mobile app that helps Indians abroad get through their first 30 days: what to do next, and who to ask.

Role
Solo: survey, interviews, UX and UI, prototype
Timeline
Apr 2026 · 2 weeks
Subject
User Interface Design
Programme
M.Des IUxD, Dhirubhai Ambani University
Mentor
Prof. Suraj Joshi
Stage
Design system and clickable prototype

on this page

  1. — at a glance
  2. 01 – how the two weeks went
  3. 02 – the question
  4. 03 – research
  5. 04 – what came up, out of 6 interviews
  6. 05 – empathy mapping
  7. 06 – signal to need
  8. 07 – problem statement
  9. 08 – from signal to feature
  10. 09 – the pivot
  11. 10 – structure
  12. 11 – user flow

  17. 16 – what’s next

at a glance

19survey responses across 8 countries
6interviews with Indians living abroad
27screens in three flows
2weeks from research to prototype

01 – how the two weeks wentResearch, define, ideate, design, prototype.

Five stages, each with a concrete output.

  1. ResearchSurvey (19) and interviews (6), then an empathy map.
  2. Define7 insights, a problem statement and How Might We questions.
  3. Ideate51 ideas sorted into 4 priority tiers, and the pivot.
  4. DesignA design system with 19 components and 27 screens.
  5. Prototype3 clickable flows and a test plan.

02 – the questionWho do you ask when everything is new?

In the words of the people surveyed and interviewed.

Everything was new: language, culture and systems.

Day 1

The first week was stressful with accommodation and registration.

Week 1

I don’t want to bother others too much.

Any day

Managing expenses was hard.

Month 3

03 – research19 survey responses, 6 interviews.

Trust came out ahead of everything else.

79%

put trust above speed, cost and convenience. 15 of 19 people surveyed.

68%

got through their first two weeks on friends and relatives. 13 of 19.

58%

use no app at all for life abroad. 11 of 19.

04 – what came up, out of 6 interviews

“No one has an obligation to help you. I try my hardest to figure it out myself, and only then do I ask for help.” — Interview participant, on asking for help

  1. Loneliness or finding friends4 of 6
  2. Money3 of 6
  3. Indian or vegetarian food3 of 6
  4. Finding a job2 of 6
  5. Accommodation1 of 6

05 – empathy mappingNewcomers don’t lack information, they lack someone to trust.

Primary user: an Indian student or worker in their first year abroad. What newcomers say, think, do and feel.

Says

“I usually Google it.” “I ask my friends or seniors when I’m stuck.” “It’s hard to trust strangers for help.” “Information is available, but not always clear.” “Finding Indian or vegetarian food is difficult.”

Thinks

Am I doing this the right way? I don’t want to bother others too much. I wish I had someone experienced here. I don’t know who to trust here. What if I make the wrong decision?

Does

Searches Google or YouTube first. Asks friends, relatives and seniors. Uses Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram for housing, food and events. Relies on trial and error. Avoids asking strangers directly.

Feels

Confused in the early stages. Lonely and isolated. Relieved when guided by someone trusted. More confident when they “know someone”. Homesick.

06 – signal to needTrust comes first.

The pattern: “I usually Google it.” Until Google isn’t enough. Search → doubt → hesitate → trial and error.

Trust comes first

It outranks speed, cost and convenience when people need help abroad.

Known beats available

People rely on the few contacts they already have, not the many sources they can find.

Asking has a cost

Nobody wants to be the newcomer who keeps bothering people.

07 – problem statementIndians in their first month abroad need a trusted way to work out what to do next and who to ask.

Because the information they find is unclear and unverified, and the people they trust are few and uncomfortable to keep asking.

08 – from signal to featureFrom what people said to what got built.

Signal → need → opportunity → feature.

  1. “It’s hard to trust strangers for help.”Know who is real → make verification visible → verified profiles and badges.
  2. “There’s a lot of trial and error in the beginning.”Know what to do, in order → a dated plan → first 30 days plan and task guides.
  3. “I don’t want to bother others too much.”Ask without imposing → helpers who opted in → ask someone who’s done it.
  4. “Finding Indian or vegetarian food is difficult.”Find the familiar nearby → a local map of what the community knows → Explore: food and grocery.
  5. “Main issue: finance.”Handle money and work after month one → guidance timed to when it bites → months 2–3 tasks.
  6. “Calling family again and again because of loneliness.”Belong somewhere local → city community and events → Explore: community.

09 – the pivotVersion 1 was emergency-led. Version 2 puts settling in first.

The survey never asked about emergencies.

Version 1 · Emergency-led

One scenario: stopped by police, no idea who to call. About 20 screens of SOS and legal help. Covered about 3 of 25 Priority 1 features.

Version 2 · Settling-in first

The first 30 days become the hero flow. Every pain point people named was about settling in. SOS stays on every screen, at the edge instead of the centre.

10 – structureEverything one tap from Home.

Splash and three intro screens, sign up or log in, onboarding, then Home: your plan, helpers, Explore and Profile.

From Home: the task guide with steps, what to bring and reminders; your first 30 days with weeks and months and the option to add your own task; helpers matched by background, verified, with ready prompts and encrypted chat; Explore for housing, food and grocery, community and money and work; and SOS with legal help, safety and verified NGOs.

11 – user flowOne flow: from arriving to the first task done.

Entry: open the app → three onboarding screens → sign up or log in → arrival setup → Home.

First task: Home → task guide → stuck on a step? Ask someone → helper profile → chat → back to the guide with an answer → mark as done → task complete → Home, next task. SOS is one tap from every screen in both lanes.

12 – design systemA calm palette with one loud colour.

Red is reserved for SOS, so it always means the same thing. Inter throughout: Display 28, H1 22, H2 18, Body 16/14, Caption 12. Nothing below 12.

Urgency · #BF1215

SOS only.

Surface · #D8DFE9

Cards and panels.

Positive · #CFDECA

Done and verified states.

Highlight · #EFF0A3

What to look at next.

Ink · #212121

Text.

Base · #F6F5FA

Background.

13 – 19 components

Every colour and text style bound to a variable.

Labels, task titles, meta, SOS and Verified badges, helper cards with what you share, and the chat bubble: each built once and reused across the 27 screens.

14 – the core flowFrom Home to a finished task.

Six screens, one bank account. This is the journey the whole app is built around.

1 · Home

The next task is the first thing you see: Open a bank account, about 30 min, 4 documents to bring.

2 · Your plan

Eight tasks in the order that makes each one easier, across week 1, week 2, month 1 and months 2–3.

3 · Task guide

Steps and documents in plain English, confirmed by 14 people in Sydney.

4 · Ask someone

Verified people who did this task in your city, with how fast they reply.

5 · Chat

A ready first message, so asking feels easy. Messages are end-to-end encrypted.

6 · Done

Progress moves on, the guide gets confirmed, and you can thank your helper in one tap.

15 – months 2 and 3Money and work get harder after the first month.

Budgeting and part-time job guides open in week 5.

Guidance is timed to when it bites: the plan keeps going after the first 30 days with the tasks people told us they struggled with later.

16 – what’s nextNot yet tested with users. That is the next step.

Five people who moved abroad in the last 12 months, five tasks, 20 minutes each on the prototype.

The first task: “You landed in Sydney yesterday. Find out what to do first.”

17 – what I learned

Three things I would carry into the next project.

A vivid scenario can pull a project away from its data

The police-stop story was memorable, so I designed for it. The survey was about bank accounts and loneliness.

The inconvenient finding was the useful one

I wanted guided flows to replace search. 53% said information alone is enough. That put the guide in front.

Twenty-five top priorities is no priority

Cutting Priority 1 from 25 features to 8 made a complete, testable flow possible in two weeks.

Keeping a small dog calm while you groom it, without needing a third hand.

Calm · reward · groom. A phygital engagement grooming dispenser for small dogs, built for Petverse.

on this page

  2. 01 – overview
  3. 02 – why Petverse
  4. 03 – benchmark

  7. 06 – primary and secondary users

the study at a glance

2ndmost difficult pet-care task: grooming
2hands needed, both already busy
3cues: light, sound, treat
1click to reward

01 – overview

Modern pet care goes beyond food and shelter to health, safety, activity, hygiene and emotional well-being. Grooming is where all of these collide.

For a Phygital Design brief, we designed for Petverse, an Indian smart pet care brand whose range covers feeders, water fountains, litter boxes and grooming tools, all minimal, premium and built for modern pet parents.

GroomCue is a small device that sits on the grooming table. It keeps a small dog calm and looking forward with a soft light, a sound cue and a treat the groomer releases with one click, so grooming can carry on with both hands.

02 – why Petverse

The brand fit for a phygital project.

Smart pet care

A strong focus on technology-driven products for everyday pet parenting.

Minimal and premium

A clean product language that a tabletop device could sit inside.

Physical + digital

Products that already pair hardware with an app, so a connected version has a home.

03 – benchmark

Dyson Pet Grooming Kit, taken apart feature by feature.

  1. Smart featuresRemoves loose hair straight into the vacuum, flexible hose, trigger-controlled suction. No connectivity or digital controls.
  2. Ease of useQuick-release attachment, lightweight brush, one-handed operation.
  3. Pet comfortAngled stainless-steel bristles reach the undercoat gently; designed for medium and long-haired dogs.
  4. The gapDyson solves the hair. Nothing in the kit helps with the dog's attention, which is what makes grooming alone so hard.

04 – research

A Google Form survey of dog owners, then a close look at the existing grooming routine.

  1. Grooming is the 2nd hardest taskAfter health monitoring, owners ranked grooming as the most difficult part of pet care.
  2. Grooming alone is difficultOwners struggle because they must manage the dog while handling grooming tools at the same time.
  3. Both hands are occupiedOne hand holds the tool; the other holds, calms, repositions or rewards the dog. "I need both hands free but I only have two."

05 – the existing ecosystem

Prepare → position → groom → manage → reward → continue.

We mapped the grooming session as a loop. "Manage" and "reward" interrupt "groom" every few seconds: the groomer stops, calms the dog, offers a treat, repositions it and starts again.

The reality: the dog loses attention, the groomer loses a hand, and the session takes twice as long as the grooming itself.

06 – primary and secondary users

L
LailaPrimary user · Shih Tzu

Receives care from her parent. Responds to touch, voice and rewards; seeks attention and reassurance; moves and reacts based on comfort and interest.

Goals
Feel safe
Get attention and rewards
Pain points
Losing interest
Being held still
Unfamiliar tools
T
The pet parentSecondary user · owner / groomer

Provides care for the dog. Grooms, handles and positions; uses voice, touch and treats to communicate; rewards cooperative behaviour.

Goals
Finish the groom calmly
Keep the dog engaged
Pain points
Only two hands
Rewarding takes attention
Grooming and engagement compete

07 – opportunity

Three things we kept seeing.

Attention is hard to sustain

A small dog looks away within seconds unless something holds its gaze.

Rewarding needs the groomer

Every treat means putting the tool down.

Two jobs, one person

Grooming and engagement compete for the same attention.

08 – how might we

How might we keep the dog engaged during grooming without adding another task for the groomer?

That question set the brief: whatever we built had to work with one click, or no clicks at all, and had to speak to the dog, not the person.

09 – what the research says

We read up on how dogs respond to sound and colour before designing a single cue.

  1. Sound gets attentionShort, distinct auditory cues can orient a dog toward a desired action. Dogs are highly responsive to sound, and the type of sound shifts attention, arousal and stress.
  2. Classical music calmsKrupa et al., 2025: 15 companion dogs showed calmer behaviour during bathing, drying, clipping and nail trimming when classical music played.
  3. Genre mattersBowman et al., 2017: 38 kennelled dogs rested more and stood less with music, with some genres producing stronger effects.
  4. Dogs see blue and yellowDogs are most sensitive to blue–yellow wavelengths. Roy et al., 2025 ("Ready, set, yellow!"): Indian free-ranging dogs approached a yellow object first, even when the grey one held food.

10 – design principles

What the research turned into.

Yellow for attentionSound to orientCalm, not startleOne click to rewardGroomer keeps both hands

11 – the concept

GroomCue: a home-friendly tabletop companion with three cues and one button.

Treat outlet: gravity-fed single treat release, so the dog gets one reward, not a handful.

Push button: a manual release trigger on the groomer-facing side, pressed with a knuckle while holding the brush.

LED ring cue: an amber 12-dot attention circle, because yellow is what dogs look at.

Audio cue: a DFPlayer directional speaker that plays calming music during the groom and a short cue before each treat.

Adjustable height: a 2-position telescopic stem, so the light sits at eye level for a Shih Tzu or a slightly taller dog.

12 – the new ecosystem

Three roles around one table.

Owner / groomer

Grooms the dog and triggers rewards with one click.

Physical companion

Provides light, sound and treats to engage the dog.

Dog

Stays focused, receives reward and feels reassured. Grooming continues while engagement happens alongside it.

13 – embedded electronic system

What is inside the prototype.

  1. Power12 V adapter, 5 V buck converter and an ON/OFF switch.
  2. InputA push button for the treat and the main power.
  3. ControllerArduino Uno R3 running the cue sequence.
  4. SoundDFPlayer Mini MP3 module with a micro-SD card and an 8 Ω speaker.
  5. LightA 12-dot amber LED ring.
  6. TreatA servo-driven gate that drops one treat per press.

14 – what works today

The current version focuses on the core interaction: continuous light + sound and manually triggered treat dispensing.

Due to prototype constraints, sensing and adaptation are not built yet. Everything the dog experiences, the groomer controls with one button.

15 – potential future versions

Where the product could go.

Smart GroomCue

Adaptive engagement: detect movement or loss of attention and adjust reward timing or change the audio based on engagement.

Connected GroomCue

A personalised grooming companion inside a larger digital ecosystem: a mobile app with dog profiles, treat tracking, saved preferences and session history.

Modes

Calm mode, reward mode and grooming mode, with favourite audio and treat preferences per dog.

16 – road-map ahead

Three things next.

  1. Refine the physical prototypeA more compact enclosure, a more consistent treat mechanism, a tray that is easier to clean and refill, and a safer, more robust build for repeated use.
  2. Engagement systemMultiple audio tracks instead of one, and different light sequences.
  3. Sensing and adaptationAdapt reward timing to the dog's behaviour.

17 – what I learned

Design for the dog first, and the groomer gets their hands back.

Every good decision came from asking what the dog can see and hear, not what the owner would like. Yellow, short sounds and one treat at a time came straight from the papers we read.

Building the electronics taught us how much a "simple" cue costs in power, timing and wiring, and why the first version had to be manual.

The full case study is on its way.

Full case study coming soon

Auto Story Table ∙ human factors in interactive dining

Capturing the table's best moments, so nobody has to reach for a phone.

A 360° café centrepiece that turns shared moments into ready-to-post stories, with opt-in privacy controls so diners stay present.

Role
Human factors research, product concept, interaction design
Timeline
Mar 2026 · 4 weeks
Team
Solo
Context
Human factors in interactive dining
Tools
Figma, FigJam, Blender for the centrepiece mockup
Status
Concept

on this page

  1. — the study at a glance
  2. 01 – overview
  3. 02 – goals
  4. 03 – research
  5. 04 – what diners said
  6. 05 – key insights
  7. 06 – how it works
  8. 07 – privacy by design
  9. 08 – testing
  10. 09 – what changes
  11. 10 – what I learned

the study at a glance

12café tables observed
6diner interviews
4 minaverage time a phone was held up per meal
0photos stored without consent

01 – overview

At cafés, people pause the moment to film it. Someone holds up a phone, the conversation stops and one person ends up behind the camera instead of at the table.

Auto Story Table is a 360° centrepiece that does the filming for the group, picks the best moments and delivers a short story before the bill arrives.

The hard part is not the camera. It is consent, presence and making sure nobody at the next table ends up in your story.

02 – goals

What the concept had to prove.

Stay present

Capture the moment without anyone leaving it.

Opt in, visibly

Nobody is recorded without knowing and agreeing, including the next table.

Worth posting

The output should be good enough that people would actually share it.

03 – research

Observation, interviews and a privacy review.

  1. ObservationWatched twelve tables across one evening at two cafés, timing how long phones were held up and who was behind the camera.
  2. InterviewsSix diners on why they film, what they do with it, and how they would feel about a table that films them.
  3. Privacy reviewRead India's DPDP Act guidance and café CCTV norms to set the consent rules.
  4. Human factorsMapped sightlines, table sizes and light levels to work out where a centrepiece could see everyone.

04 – what diners said

Two reactions that set the rules.

I want the memory, I don't want to be the one making it.

Diner, 24

If I didn't say yes, it shouldn't exist. And I want to know when it's on.

Diner, 31

05 – key insights

What the research made clear.

The photographer misses the moment

One person at every table was out of the conversation while filming.

Consent must be visible

People accepted being filmed only if there was a clear signal it was on and a way to say no.

Food is the trigger

The arrival of a dish is when every table reached for a phone.

06 – how it works

Six steps from centrepiece to story.

  1. The setupA 360° sensor sits at the centre of the table and sees every angle at once. An amber ring shows when it is active.
  2. The momentAI notices a hero dish arriving and records the food and the group together.
  3. The interactionThe system digitally pans to the speaker or the action, with no moving parts.
  4. The processingThe engine picks the best angles, removes fish-eye distortion and crops to 9:16 and 16:9.
  5. The notificationThe story is compiled and sent to the people who opted in, before the bill arrives.
  6. The final exportA multi-perspective story, ready to share, with every face outside the table blurred.

07 – privacy by design

The rules the concept is built on.

Opt in per person

Each diner taps their phone to the centrepiece to join. No tap, no face.

Visible state

The amber ring means recording; off means off. No hidden mode.

Nothing kept

Raw footage is deleted after the story is built. Only the people who opted in get a copy.

08 – testing

A staged dinner with a mock centrepiece.

  1. MethodSix people, one table, a camera rig standing in for the centrepiece. Measured phone-up time and asked about comfort afterwards.
  2. ResultPhone-up time fell from about 4 minutes to under 30 seconds. All six said the amber ring made them comfortable; two asked to opt out mid-meal and did.

09 – what changes

Staged dinner, before and after.

beforeafter
Phone held up per meal~4 min→< 30 s
People out of the conversation1 per table→0
ConsentAssumed→Per person, visible
Faces outside the tableCaptured→Blurred

10 – what I learned

The product is the consent model. The camera is the easy part.

Every design decision that worked came from the privacy rules, not from the technology.

Next: a working prototype with a real 360° camera and a test in a café with the owner's and diners' consent.

The full case study is on its way.

Full case study coming soon
